what_its_for: Carbamazepine is used to control certain types of seizures (epilepsy), treat nerve pain in the face called trigeminal neuralgia, and manage mood swings in bipolar disorder. Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions.
how_to_take: Take carbamazepine exactly as your doctor tells you. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water — do not crush or chew extended-release tablets or capsules. You can open extended-release capsules (Carbatrol) and sprinkle the beads on soft food like applesauce, but do not chew the beads. Take this medicine with food or milk to reduce stomach upset. Try to take it at the same times every day to keep a steady level in your body.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it over time. The dose depends on your condition, age, weight, and how your body responds. Never change your dose or stop taking this medicine on your own — stopping suddenly can cause serious problems, including seizures. Always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store carbamazepine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use medicine that is expired — ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking carbamazepine — it can increase dizziness and drowsiness and may affect your seizure control. Do not eat grapefruit or drink grapefruit juice, as it can raise the level of this medicine in your blood and cause serious side effects. Be careful driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid starting new medicines, vitamins, or herbal supplements without asking your doctor or pharmacist first, as many drugs interact with carbamazepine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: a skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin (this can be a sign of a rare but dangerous reaction); swelling of your face, lips, or throat; signs of low blood cell counts such as unusual bruising, bleeding, fever, chills, or feeling very tired; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); dark urine; confusion, unusual mood changes, or thoughts of hurting yourself; vision changes or unsteady walking; or signs of an allergic reaction. Tell your doctor at all regular visits so your blood levels and blood counts can be checked.
when_it_works: It may take several weeks before carbamazepine reaches the right level in your body and you feel its full benefit. For seizures, you may notice fewer episodes over several weeks. For nerve pain, some people feel relief within a few days. For bipolar disorder, mood improvements may take longer. Do not stop taking it even if you feel well — this medicine works best when taken every day as prescribed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Carbamazepine can harm an unborn baby, including causing birth defects. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Use effective birth control while taking this medicine. Breastfeeding: This medicine passes into breast milk. Ask your doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while taking carbamazepine. Children: This medicine can be used in children for seizures, but dosing is based on weight and age. Children should be closely monitored. Older adults: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness, confusion, and low sodium levels and may need a lower dose. Asian patients: People of Asian ancestry (especially those from China, Thailand, Malaysia, Philippines, Taiwan, or Korea) should be tested for a gene called HLA-B*1502 before starting carbamazepine, as they have a higher risk of a very serious and potentially life-threatening skin reaction. Ask your doctor about this test.
